claims.text: The initial Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy contains a metastable, non-equilibrium solid solution.
Controlled thermal aging causes Mg-rich intermetallic compounds to nucleate and grow.
The nucleation and growth of Mg-rich intermetallic compounds are diffusion-controlled.
Moderate aging produces fine, uniformly distributed Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates.
Fine, uniformly distributed intermetallic precipitates promote a continuous MgO-enriched passivating layer.
A continuous MgO-enriched passivating layer retains or enhances corrosion resistance.
A continuous MgO-enriched passivating layer retains or enhances high-temperature oxidation resistance.
More aggressive thermal exposure causes intermetallic precipitate coarsening.
Coarsened precipitates disrupt matrix continuity.
Coarsened precipitates disrupt protective oxide-film continuity.
Loss of matrix and oxide-film continuity degrades corrosion resistance.
Loss of matrix and oxide-film continuity degrades high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Moderately aged samples will retain or slightly improve corrosion resistance relative to the as-cast state.
Moderately aged samples will retain or slightly improve high-temperature oxidation resistance relative to the as-cast state.
Higher-temperature or longer-duration aging will produce coarser intermetallic precipitates and measurably lower corrosion and oxidation protection.
The as-cast baseline has a homogeneous elemental distribution and initial protective properties.
The proposed pathway applies when thermal exposure initiates intermetallic formation but remains below complete homogenization.
The transition to degraded performance occurs when aging produces coarse, discontinuous precipitates.
Reported behavior in Mg-containing alloys supports the proposed fine-versus-coarse intermetallic trend and its relationship to protective properties.
The temperature and time thresholds for the transition depend on alloy composition and environmental factors.
